title: How do you know a thermal lens will perform? Inside optical testing
summary: See how LightPath uses glass characterization, surface profilometry, and final lens MTF testing to verify thermal lens optical performance.
body_markdown:
A thermal camera may have the detector resolution an application requires and still struggle to deliver useful detail. The lens must collect infrared energy and form an image with enough contrast for the camera to distinguish the features that matter.


An optical design predicts how a lens should perform. Testing establishes how the manufactured lens performs under defined conditions.


Our articles on[scaling domestic optics](https://www.lightpath.com/blog/scaling-domestic-optics-for-small-uas-counter-uas-and-precision-munitions) and[designing optics for production](https://www.lightpath.com/blog/from-prototype-to-production-designing-optics-that-can-be-built-at-scale) explored the manufacturing processes and engineering decisions behind repeatable production. Optical testing provides the evidence that connects those decisions to the finished product.


At LightPath, that work includes material characterization, measurement of individual lens surfaces, and testing of the completed optical assembly. Each stage answers a different question about performance.


**Start With the Glass**


Infrared lens design begins with understanding the optical material. Engineers need to know how the glass bends light so they can design surfaces and arrange elements to bring that light into focus.


Refractive index describes that behavior. Accurate material data helps engineers develop an optical prescription suited to the glass.


LightPath’s Glass Analytics Lab in Orlando provides testing and instrumentation resources for material characterization and qualification. Located in a separate suite from production, the lab supports understanding the glass itself.


Its in-house refractometry capability measures the refractive index of infrared glass at room temperature. This connects material development with the optical data engineers need when designing lenses around that glass.


Material characterization establishes design inputs. Verifying the manufactured lens requires further measurements: first at the individual element, then at the finished assembly.


**Check Surface Form Before Assembly**


Once glass becomes a lens element, its surfaces must match the shapes specified in the optical design within the allowed tolerances.


At LightPath, a profilometer measures the surface profile of individual lens elements before they enter an assembly. Comparing the measured profile with the intended design form helps identify departures that could affect optical performance.


Catching a form error at this stage allows the manufacturing team to address it at its source, before the element moves into an assembly. That provides a clearer opportunity to correct the problem and avoids carrying it into later manufacturing steps.


Surface form also needs to be distinguished from other surface characteristics. Surface quality concerns imperfections such as scratches and pits, while roughness describes finer surface texture. These characteristics can affect light differently and require appropriate specifications and inspection methods.[Edmund Optics’ guide to optical specifications](https://www.edmundoptics.co.uk/knowledge-center/application-notes/optics/understanding-optical-specifications/) explains these distinctions.


A surface that looks clean can still depart from its intended shape. Measuring its profile gives engineers evidence that visual inspection alone cannot provide.


**Alignment Connects Individual Elements to Assembly Performance**


An optical assembly depends on the placement of its elements as well as their individual quality.


Spacing, tilt, and decenter influence how light travels through the lens. Decenter shifts an element away from its intended axis; tilt changes its angular orientation. Variations in these positions can affect focus and image quality.


As discussed in our article on[designing optics that can be built at scale](https://www.lightpath.com/blog/from-prototype-to-production-designing-optics-that-can-be-built-at-scale) , tolerances define how much variation the design can accommodate. Mechanical features and assembly processes help control that variation.


This is why component measurements and final assembly testing serve complementary purposes. A surface profile establishes whether an individual surface meets its form requirement. Testing the completed lens evaluates the combined optical result after the elements have been assembled.


If the finished lens falls outside its performance limits, component measurements provide useful evidence for investigating the cause.


**MTF Connects Contrast to Detail**


Modulation transfer function, or MTF, describes how well a lens preserves contrast at different levels of detail.


Larger features may remain distinguishable even when finer features blur together. An MTF curve shows how contrast transfer changes as the features become smaller.[Edmund Optics’ introduction to MTF](https://www.edmundoptics.com/knowledge-center/application-notes/optics/introduction-to-modulation-transfer-function/) explains the relationship between contrast, resolution, and optical performance.


For a thermal camera, preserving contrast helps retain differences between neighboring scene features. The lens must deliver enough optical detail for the detector and the application.


A useful MTF requirement specifies the conditions being evaluated, including the spatial frequencies, field positions, wavelength band, aperture, and focus conditions. Those conditions give the measurement meaning and allow engineers to compare results against the intended performance.


**Test the Finished Lens**


At final assembly, LightPath measures the MTF of the finished lens to verify that it meets the contrast and resolution requirements specified for the customer’s system.


This measurement evaluates the optical performance of the assembled lens. It captures the combined result of the manufactured elements and their assembly under the test conditions.


The two confirmed stages of LightPath’s lens testing work together:


- **Before assembly, profilometry verifies surface form.** Measuring individual lens elements helps identify errors while they can be addressed at the component level.
- **At final assembly, MTF testing verifies optical performance.** Measuring the completed lens confirms whether it meets its specified image-quality requirements.


Together, these measurements give customers confidence that the finished lens meets its specified optical performance requirements. They also provide manufacturing teams with information at more than one stage, helping them investigate discrepancies between component quality and assembled performance.


**Material Characterization and Lens Testing in Orlando**


LightPath’s material characterization and lens metrology activities have distinct roles and locations within its Orlando operations.


The Glass Analytics Lab handles material characterization and qualification in its separate suite. Metrology for manufactured lenses takes place in production, primarily in the cleanroom or Diamond Turning room.


That distinction connects each measurement to the question it answers. Refractometry supplies information about the infrared glass. Profilometry verifies the form of a manufactured lens surface. MTF testing evaluates the image-forming performance of the completed lens.


These activities support different stages of LightPath’s[optical design and manufacturing capabilities](https://www.lightpath.com/capabilities) , linking material knowledge with fabrication and finished-product verification.


For an OEM, understanding those stages makes the testing discussion more useful: Which properties are being measured? At what point in manufacturing? Under which conditions? And against which acceptance limits?


**Connect Lens Measurements to Usable Imagery**


A verified lens gives the camera system a stronger foundation for producing useful imagery. The complete result also depends on the detector, electronics, image processing, and operating environment.


Lens MTF therefore belongs within a broader verification plan. It establishes optical performance under defined conditions, while camera and application testing evaluate how the integrated system performs in use.


Defining the optical requirements early gives the customer and supplier a shared basis for acceptance. It also connects manufacturing measurements to the features the camera needs to resolve.


From room-temperature refractive-index measurement to surface profilometry and final assembly MTF, each stage contributes evidence. Together, they help engineers move from a lens designed to perform to a manufactured lens with measured performance.
